checked: The summary names the subject directly; prose avoids the listed stock phrases and varies its openings.
Example #1 uses rational form p/q from the number-set definitions in Core Concept.
Example #2 uses i^1=i, i^2=-1, i^3=-i, i^4=1 and remainder cycling, all in Core Concept/Powers of i.
Example #3 uses distributive multiplication and replacement of i^2 by -1, both taught in Core Concept/Multiplying Complex Numbers.
Example #4 uses the conjugate a-bi, product a^2+b^2, and multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate, all introduced in Core Concept/Conjugates and Division.

Examples cover classification with the zero convention, large powers, complex multiplication, and complex division. The negative-root trap additionally works a distinct root-product case. Cases progress from sets to multi-step operations without duplicate examples.
All four worked examples number their solution steps; power remainders, products, and quotient computations are displayed. The short n/1 classification justification may remain inline.
The longest displays are single expansions such as the complex product; each stays on one reasonably narrow algebra line.
Paragraphs stay within three sentences; lists are limited to useful checks or shortcuts and solution steps.

The single FIGURE comment specifies nested sets and separates irrational from rational numbers within the reals. Its semantics label resolves the flat box list, and the surrounding definitions teach the inclusion without the image.

Number sets, i, real and imaginary parts, the power cycle and remainder method are defined before examples. Conjugate is defined before division uses it; numerator and denominator are used in their ordinary fraction sense.

Multiplication explicitly distributes each term and collects real and imaginary terms. Division explains why multiplying by the conjugate preserves value and makes the denominator real. Powers and classification are explained, not merely named.

Rational denominators are nonzero; natural-number conventions are qualified. Negative-root rewriting requires positive k; the real root-product identity is limited to nonnegative inputs. Complex division forbids zero and the power-cycle method specifies positive exponents.
